06 Acceptance

We’re moving all courses to the new Self Mastery Community


Watch Video At: https://youtu.be/5cuATZL6Xa4

Summary of practice

1. Listen to the Acceptance lesson audio
You may want to listen multiple times.

2. Practice creating the relaxed feeling of acceptance (non-resistance) in
your body. Do this multiple times every day. One aspect of this exercise is to break the
pattern of adding additional layers of reaction and rejection.

3. Begin and practice a kind of mantra with your words to be accepting and
allowing of what is going on. Let your words blend into having a relaxed attitude as
best you can. Do this with things you are not able to change in this moment. It may
include being accepting of how your mind is full of chatter or different emotions you
have. You can also practice this when you are calm to reinforce this state in your
nervous system.

Some notes

The practice is about finding that relaxed feeling in your body, nervous system,
emotions, and mental state. You might not like the word “acceptance” to describe it, or
feel acceptance means something else. If it does, then find another word for you to
anchor the process to. Or it might be a phrase like “It just is what it is.”

Pay close attention to the feeling and meaning. Any word or phase can have multiple
meanings and messages to it depending on how we say it. “That was great.” can be a
compliment. However, with a sarcastic tone it is is a put down. Notice how it feels to
your nervous system and body and that will help guide you.

You generate emotions more from your body than you do from your thoughts. Your
thought might trigger a nervous system and physical response that generates emotion.
                                                                                                                                   1/4

By getting your body relaxed you are taking more control over what emotions you
generate and how you feel. This will change what part of your brain is active, the primal
fight or flight part, or the more creative consciousness parts of the brain.

In the last session on third person writing there is likely to be a push-back of emotions
and uncomfortable feelings from the ego-mind. This acceptance practice helps you
manage those push-back feelings the mind is reacting with. They need to be
acknowledged, but not acted on. Your ability to be the Observer and refrain from acting
them out is the practice.

Resistance to change

There are many ways to interpret the meaning of “acceptance.” Certain parts of your
mind will likely distort the intention. This is normal. Those parts are all revved up to
have conflict, challenges, be heroic, complain, criticize, expect too much or fight etc.
These parts of your mind and personality will get further focus in the next assignment.

For now, take our your journal and write third person about how your mind objects and
complains, procrastinates, or confuses this exercise. Use the Observer Perspective
practice of lesson 5 to step outside the resistance stories about this exercise and write
about them.

Write out what “acceptance” will mean for those different parts of the mind. Write out
the consequences of what that part of the mind imagines. While doing this you can
practice the real acceptance of just acknowledging that these thoughts, beliefs, and
emotions are there.

Watch out for any part of your being that thinks this needs immediate “change” or
“fixing.” This “rush” in to “fix” comes with some underlying rejection programs that the
practice advises you refrain from. These are all automated unconscious programs to
observe and refrain from acting on. If you act on them, you are just being a slave to your
unconscious belief programming. By practicing “acceptance” you are doing something
different, a type of calm relaxed rebellion to your automatic reactions.

Observing and refraining from these impulses is different, and different means new
neural pathways.

Common questions

What if there is stuff that I don't want to accept?
Great, that means you want to change it. However, the more you “hate, criticize, reject,
and judge” IT, the more energy you are spending on reacting to it instead of changing it.

Those expressions of rejection don’t create change. So practice refraining from
expressing your energy that way and you will have more energy to focus on what does
work.

                                                                                                                                   2/4

This is how change starts. You have to first eliminate some bad habits that interfere
with creating change.

It feels like I am giving up or surrendering to it.
If it feels like “acceptance” means giving up or surrendering to it always being there,
then the meaning and feeling isn’t clear on the practice. Spend some time writing (Third
Person of course) about what the mind believes “acceptance” is, what it means, and
what will be the results. It sounds like “acceptance” has turned into a meaning of
“failure and hopelessness.”

You will be revealing the beliefs behind these thoughts. If you are skeptical of them, you
may notice some inconsistencies in their logic.

It’s not you that doesn’t believe in acceptance, it is your unconscious beliefs, and you are
just watching them react. This is provided you remain in the Neutral Observer
Perspective.

Redefine “acceptance” as an acknowledgement of where things are in this moment. It
makes no claims or intentions about the future situation.

Can I use a different word than Acceptance?
Yes, of course. You are welcome to change the exercises to suit you. Just be sure to keep
the Intent and Feeling of the exercise as described.

Some people prefer the word, Acknowledge, or change it to,

“I’ll refrain from fighting reality right now.”

OR, “it is what it is”

There are many ways to use words and express a relaxed, non-rejecting attitude.
 Create a way that works well for you.

It doesn't seem like anything is happening?
The intent isn’t so much to dismantle big agreements right now. It is about creating an
expression that bypasses the Judge character. (more about him in the next lesson on
Characters.)

In the last session on third person writing there is likely to be a push-back of emotions
and uncomfortable feelings from that exercise. This acceptance practice helps you
manage those push-back feelings the mind is reacting with.

Relaxing the body is also important as your nervous system needs to be in a more
relaxed state for the changes that are coming.

Supporting videos



                                                                                                                                   3/4

Watch Video At: https://youtu.be/L56nq0wVF3s

Self Awareness not Self Judgement

It’s easy to see what you are doing and thinking and criticize it. Some people do this and
think they are being self aware. That’s not self awareness. Self awareness begins when
you step out of this criticizing part of the mind.

Watch Video At: https://youtu.be/2GDc42j-dNQ

How being accepting helps you change

Judgment, rejection, criticism, and other reactions can cause you to spend a lot of
energy and not go anywhere bit deeper into a pit. You can exhaust yourself in those
stories. Refrain, and you gather personal power.

Watch Video At: https://youtu.be/pVLQw8MIoow

Resistance to the Acceptance Exercise

You spend all day putting your body into small tensions that build up. Somewhere in
your unconscious you have learned that you “need” to do this. You don’t. But that part
of your unconscious beliefs will still try to “resist” because it still believes you “need”. As
if all that stress somehow helped you. It doesn’t, but you don’t know that yet.





                                                                                                                                   4/4

06 Acceptance Transcript

   pathwaytohappiness.com/courses/self-mastery-course-1/06-acceptance/06-acceptance-transcript

                                                                        May 11, 2019

The last couple of assignments, specifically “Abdication of power” and “Finding
neutral”, had us really paying attention to our words, our agreements, and the types of
things we say, and hopefully we’ve become a little more conscious of some automatic
responses that we do in conversation. Those two assignments had a lot to do with
extending our awareness, and one of the very common experiences people have, doing
these two assignments, is: “Oh my god, I can’t believe how much I do this.” Then, their
next response to this new found awareness of how much they do this, and the
significance of it, is: “Oh, I got to stop, I shouldn’t be doing this,” and they judge
themselves and are critical of themselves for doing this thing that they had no idea they
were doing until just recently. Well, this is where this acceptance practice comes in. We
have to give ourselves something to do other than this self-criticism based of this new
realization. It’s not enough that we can celebrate this new level of awareness like: “Oh, I
see what I’m doing here. I can see the effects of this. This is probably not what I want to
keep doing.” No. Our programmed response to seeing something like that is a self-
criticism, typically. This exercise on acceptance is the response to that reaction of self-
criticism.

Many different traditions and practices teach the same basic premise in a lot of
different ways. And it’s really about “being present with”, being aware and present with
really mostly just yourself and the world the way it is, and that means being with people,
and being present with them just the way they are – without judgment, without pushing
them away, which is what a judgment does in a form of rejection. This “being present
with” is the opposite to “pushing away” effect. And one of the challenging things I’m
going to ask you to do in this exercise, if you have that inner voice of the Judge that
pushes things away, is to practice to be present with that voice, to be present with those
stories in your own mind. The incredible value of this is that just by doing this, we are
practicing getting, having and keeping our own attention in the point of view of our
choice, because as long as we’re pushing away and rejecting, our point of view of
perception and our point of view of creating our life is coming from the point of view of
judgment and victimization, as we’ll find out later. Cause always when we are in that not
present state of rejecting or being judgmental, we’re creating our world by pushing
away, distancing and separating our self, and we are not being present with. So, this is
the challenge for the exercise. And probably, since the last two assignments, what you
do is exactly that kind of “pushing away” approach.

Before I get into the discussion of today’s topic, I want to first do an exercise. You can
play this tape as I talk you through this. In this exercise you need to be standing in a
room. 1) What I want you to do is just make your body relaxed, standing straight up,
and bend your body at the ankles, leaning forward. Lean your body forward, bending
only at the ankles. You’ll feel your weight shifts to the front of your feet, and you’ll be
                                                                                                                           1/10

hanging out there a little bit off balance – it’s not our normal balance. And I want you to
keep leaning forward at the ankles, as far as you can go. You’ll notice your toes are
probably gripping, and once you feel that you’re hanging up there as far as you can go,
just stop. I want you to notice how your whole body feels, and notice if you feel any
tension in your body, and lean back to straight up and down again. Put your awareness
on that tension and let all the muscles, and everything about your body and your
nervous system relax, let your shoulders drop, let your neck come loose, let your jaw
relax, notice the difference. Now your body’s standing upright, but now it’s relaxed. 2) I
want you to do this exercise again, noticing that as you lean forward, your body starts
gripping and holding tension. Starting with your body relaxed straight up and down,
bend forward, bending at the ankles, and notice how the muscles in the body start to
tense. The muscles in the body will have to tense, because it’s off balance, and certain
muscles will be gripping and tightening in order to keep you from tipping over. There
are other muscles that will also grip and tighten: you may feel the tension in your neck,
in your shoulders, in your belly, particularly in the visceral sensation in your gut. Now I
want you to notice that tension in your body, and as you come back to upright, notice
how that tension remains. Whether it’d be viscerally in your gut, in your shoulders, in
your neck, in your jaw – notice the tension that remains in your body. Now, with your
awareness on the tension in your body, actively relax your body, and let the tension go.

Notice how your arms can soften, your shoulders can soften, your jaw, your neck, and
notice how your gut, your visceral body relaxes, muscles in your legs – those that were
tense while you were leaning, and still held tension when you came back to upright –
relax. Notice how you shift all of this at your will. Your attention is on the tension when
you’re upright, and just by deciding: “Ok, I’m going to relax my body,” your whole
physical state changes. 3) I want you to do this again – leaning forward and noticing
how your muscles become more tense, but also how your visceral body tightening, or
we could say your “resistance”, comes up in your physical body. Notice how it comes up,
notice that when you lean back and stand upright again, the resistance and tension
remain. Lot of the body stays in stress, even though you’re standing upright again.

Now notice how you relax if you decide to relax, you intend it, and muscles relax and
calm down again. 4) Now we’re going to make it a little more interesting. Let your body
relax, shake up your abs, arms, legs, and then, standing upright, bending only at the
ankles, lean forward until you feel the tension and the visceral tightening – what we’ll
call “resistance”. Feel that tension and resistance build up in the body, and now, while
you’re leaning forward, I want you to intentionally relax the body in that leaning
forward position. Relax the neck, the jaw, the arms, the shoulders, the back, only leaving
engaged those muscles necessary to hold yourself balanced in this leaning forward
position, and notice how you can just relax into it. Some muscles will still be working,
but a lot of your body can relax. It’s what I’ll call just letting go of the resistance, and
accepting. Then, go ahead and stand back up.





                                                                                                                           2/10

What we learned a long ago is that if we’re off balance, we might fall, and that might be
painful, so we want to avoid that, and we fear falling. But there’s nothing wrong with
leaning forward. What we’re noticing here is our visceral reaction to the fear of falling,
where all that resistance and tension come up, opposite to when we relax, when we’re
no longer afraid of falling. We’re not going to fall over, we are standing upright, we can
easily put one foot out and catch ourselves, in case a stiff breeze comes, and it’s unlikely
a stiff breeze will come to knock us over while we’re standing in our living room, or our
kitchen, or our office. But yet we have that fear, and because we have that fear, by
conditioning, we have that tension that we call “resistance” – that tightening in our
visceral body, which then tightens the physical muscles. This all happens when we lean
over and are just a little bit off our normal standing position. 5) Again, lean forward,
notice all the tension comes in, and then allow yourself to dissolve it, while remaining
leaning forward. And you’ll see that you can let go of the tension and resistance that
come up from this idea of fear of falling, and just notice: “Yeah, I need to have some
muscles engaged while I’m leaning forward, but for the most part my body can be
relaxed, my visceral body can be relaxed, and I can be at ease.” 6) Do that a couple of
times, until you’re very skilled with that exercise of leaning forward, noticing like a
tension builds, what that visceral tightness feels like, how it spreads to your physical
tension in your muscles, and then noticing that you can control that tension and that
attitude, and relax into this new position, that previously you would have thought
uncomfortable or scaring.

That’s the exercise. That exercise is to show you how we build tension and what I call
“resistance” in your body, and how that visceral sensation, that visceral tightening can
become physical tension in the muscles, where our muscles start to grip, because our
visceral body feels tension. That’s what the resistance side of this looks like. What we’ll
call “acceptance” is that relaxing into that situation that we’re in. If we are leaning
forward and we feel that tension, we can command our body to relax in that position,
relax our arms, our shoulders, our neck, our jaw. While in that position, while our
muscles are engaged, we can relax our visceral body and relax so much of our physical
body, by just accepting and acknowledging: “Ok, this is where I am. Is there any real
danger? No, I’m not going to fall. Let me just settle in and relax to what’s going on right
now. Right now I’m just leaning forward at the ankles, and it’s no big deal.” We don’t
have to add this stress of falling down or “What’s going to happen next?” “Right now
this is just what is, and I accept that I’m just leaning forward, and I let the rest of my
body relax, and I just remain engaged in only the areas of the muscles I need to stay
standing.” So, we have the tension that we call “resistance”, and there is what we call
“acceptance”, which is the active relaxation into just what is – we call that acceptance,
and acceptance has a real visceral feeling in the body, acceptance has a real shift in our
visceral body and in our physical body in the amount of tension we hold. Acceptance is
not just an intellectual concept or point of view. Acceptance can be an action done with
our attitude, and it has an affect on our physical body. It’s an active visceral body
exercise. That’s real acceptance, where we relax into what is, even if what is has us a
little off balance.


                                                                                                                           3/10

I wanted to do that exercise first, so that we can specifically understand when I use the
word “acceptance”, what am I talking about, and when I use the word “resistance”, what
I am talking about. Resistance actually has a feeling, it’s actually a sensation in our
visceral body, and we then also feel it physically. It has an emotional component. Any
kind of experience like that we feel viscerally, we feel physically, has emotional
component, and it may feel a little bit edgy. Acceptance – that shifting of your attitude
to a place of acceptance and just acknowledging: “Ok, here I am, I’m just leaning
forward, I’m in a perfectly safe room, there aren’t going to be any strong winds to blow
me off balance, I don’t have to worry about falling down, cause I know how to catch
myself. My knees work, my legs work, there’s nobody here to push me, so I can just
relax into this body.” Then we let go of that extra stress and tension, and acceptance
becomes just settling into and relaxing into where we are right now, and letting go of the
fear of the idea of what might happen, such as falling down. This fear of falling down is
something we’re playing in our imagination. It’s a scenario we learnt years and years
ago, that’s part of the programmed response of our visceral body, and it’s what we’re
fearing, but what we’re fearing is that virtual reality creation of what might happen, say
falling down. This is why our body is tightened and our visceral body is tightened, and it
has more to do with when we fell down at 1 or 2 years old, than with what’s really going
on in the room today. For a little refresher on the power of this virtual reality you might
go back to session two and listen to the first meditation awareness exercise I did during
the “Autobiography” session.

Your mission, for the next few weeks, should you choose to accept it, is to actively
practice acceptance throughout the day as many times a day as you can: every five
minutes, every thirty minutes, every hour, whatever is you schedule that works for you,
to just notice what your physical body is feeling, to notice where the tension is in your
body, to notice your visceral body and your emotional state, and to relax into it and say:
“Ok, for whatever else is going on in the world right now, I am right here, let me relax
into and just be right here and right now, and let go of any fears of where this thing
might go that I may find tension about.”

One of the assignments I gave myself as I learnt to practice acceptance is I got a mala
(basically Hindu version of rosary beads, prayer beads), and throughout the day, I
would say: “I accept life as it is, I accept life as it is and relax into my body, I accept life
is just the way it is, and I accept myself just the way I am, I accept that, and I would fill
in whatever is going on throughout the day, and I would be aware what is going on with
my physical and visceral sensations, and my emotional sensations.” I had to consciously
teach myself acceptance, and I taught myself through repeating the story “I accept life
as it is,” and filling in whatever was going on about life at that time. This is what I want
you to do to practice acceptance. You can say the words, give yourself a mantra when
that works for you, but at the same time relax into your body, relax into your visceral
body, relax into your emotional body.





                                                                                                                           4/10

As I give this assignment to some people, they sometimes say: “Oh, it’s surrendering,”
but I don’t really want to use that word. That word has a lot of other meanings, and one
of them means “to give up”, and I don’t want to go and take ourselves in that direction
at this time. Acceptance doesn’t mean “to give up”. Acceptance is more “to
acknowledge”. Some people resist using the word “acceptance”: “I accept life”, “I accept
what’s going on”, because they find out they have in their mind that by accepting, they
agree with it and give in to it. They say: “Ok, I accept,” as in “I give in,” but this is not the
way we’re using “acceptance”. We are using acceptance more in a way of “I
acknowledge, this is where I am, and this is what’s going on.” It’s an honest assessment
of life as it is and a letting go of what might come. Because what might come is not life
as it is, but life as we imagine, or as our fears imagine, and the way our imagination
projects, and that’s what we’re letting go of. We are saying: “Ok, I’m letting go of that,
and I’m just being here right now with what is.” And we could say that in a certain sense
“acceptance” does mean “give up”, it does mean “surrender”, but what we’re specifically
surrendering is our attachment to, or our clinging to what the virtual reality in our
mind, what the imagination is dreaming of. That’s what we’re letting go of, that’s what
we’re surrendering, that’s what we’re giving up. And in that way of giving up that virtual
reality projection, we’re embracing, and being present with what’s really happening
right now in life, and with what just really is right now.

You can also use the word “acknowledge”, if acceptance means too much like “give up”:
“I am aware of and I am relaxing into that experience, and I am not fighting with, and
I’m not resisting life as it is.” That’s what we’re accomplishing, that’s what I want you to
do over and over, and over again throughout the day.

One way to help you do this over and over again is like I said – to get a mala and to
repeat to yourself: “I accept life as it is.” And I would just repeat that: “I accept life as it
is,” as a practice. And we’ll get into why this has big effects in a little bit, because it kind
of seems silly to note the obvious, but the practice, the visceral practicing of learning
how to accept and relax into life as it is a huge feat.

I was teaching a seminar and I was showing people how to do this with their physical
body. And I was actually having people do this with partners, when they pushed on each
other, and while someone’s pushing on you, you relax into it, you stay engaged with
your muscles, and yet you let the rest of your body relax and be melted, and your
visceral body be unstressed. And a woman told me later that she knew all this, she knew
about acceptance and relaxing from her yoga class, from her martial arts class, but she
hadn’t done it in a very long time. She knew she should be accepting the things, but she
wasn’t doing it, until that class, and she said: “Ok, now I know what this feels like
again.” And making this action, where she actually took the action to melt into, relax
into what was going on, changed her point of view. That changed her whole state, it
changed her attitude, it changed her emotional state, it changed the way she felt in her
body physically. That is the action we are going to master – to be able to shift our point
of view, to be of total acceptance. At first smaller things in life, and later greater and
greater things, until we accept life as it is.

                                                                                                                           5/10

Simple places to start: “I accept this is my body. And it is what it is. It’s the height that it
is, it’s the weight that it is.” And acceptance doesn’t mean: “I agree this is my body and
I’m forever going to be this way and hide”. Acceptance means: “I acknowledge this is
what my body looks like right now.” And if I’m driving in my car: “I accept this is the
condition of traffic, I accept this is the weather, that it’s bright and sunny, and I accept
that it’s rainy and cloudy.” And this is just looking at life and saying: “I acknowledge it
the way it is, and I accept it the way it is,” and “I accept people the way they are,” and “I
accept that this person does this, and this is what they do, and this is their behavior, and
this is their patterned routine. I acknowledge and I accept it’s just the way it is. Why?
Because it’s just the way it is.”

When I say that I had to give myself this exercise and that I had to consciously commit
to doing this over and over, and over, it’s because I had another story running, and that
story was the Judge’s story, and the Judge’s story was: “I reject, I reject, I reject”: I
